subject: MGMT160
title: Managing Change, Innovation and the Future of Work

questions.stem: Describe organisational change.
options: Altering how the organisation works — its strategy, structure, technology, people or processes
Changing the company logo, colours and uniforms so that customers notice a fresh image in the shops
Replacing the top manager and the leadership team with people from outside the company
Moving to a bigger office or a new building when the current one is too small for the staff
questions.why: Five things can change; usually people are the hardest part. See §8.1.

questions.stem: Identify the five pressures that force organisations to change.
options: Competition, technology, customer expectations, globalisation, economic changes
Fear, uncertainty, comfort with old ways, loss of control and loss of status among staff
Planning, organising, leading, controlling, innovating
Salaries, offices, managers, customers, suppliers
questions.why: Chapter 3's environment never stops moving. See §8.1.

questions.stem: Explain the success trap.
options: The better today's business performs, the harder it is to change it
Successful companies have no competitors to watch
Success makes managers lazy about profits, so costs rise until the company fails
Successful companies cannot hire good people, because talented staff prefer start-ups
questions.why: Nokia perfected yesterday's phone; Kodak protected film against its own digital invention. See §8.1.

questions.stem: Identify the four honest reasons people resist change.
options: Fear, uncertainty, comfort with old ways, loss of control or status
Laziness, lack of intelligence, disloyalty, old age and stubbornness
Low pay, long hours, bad managers and small offices
Competition, technology, globalisation and the economy
questions.why: Resistance is information about what people are protecting, not disloyalty. See §8.2.

questions.stem: Explain how a manager should treat resistance.
options: As information about what people are protecting — read it and fix the plan
As disloyalty to be punished
As proof that the employees are too old for the new way and should be replaced
As a sign that the change should be cancelled, because the team knows the work best
questions.why: The manager who treats resistance as disloyalty hardens it; the manager who reads it fixes the plan. See §8.2.

questions.stem: Identify the four tools for managing resistance, in order.
options: Communication, participation, training, support
Punishment, pressure, strict deadlines and bonuses
Email announcement, manual, launch and review
Hire, dismiss, train and promote
questions.why: Communicate why first, involve second, train before launch, support through the dip. See §8.3.

questions.stem: Explain why the order of the four tools matters.
options: Nobody wants training for a change they do not understand, and people only train for a design they had a say in
Training is the most expensive of the four tools, so it comes last to protect the budget in case the change is cancelled
Support should always come first, because people need to feel safe before they will listen to anything
The order does not matter, as long as all four tools are used at some point during the change
questions.why: Communicate first, involve second, then train, then support. See §8.3.

questions.stem: Explain what 'support' means in managing change.
options: Patience in the dip — performance drops before it rises, and punishing the dip kills the change
Paying a bonus to every employee who accepts the change within the first month
Sending more emails and reminders to every employee so that nobody can say they were not informed about the change
Hiring a consultant to run the change so that the manager can concentrate on the daily work
questions.why: Every real change has a dip. See §8.3.

questions.stem: Identify Lewin's three steps in order.
options: Unfreeze → change → refreeze
Plan → do → check
Announce → train → review
Refreeze → change → unfreeze
questions.why: Create readiness, make the move, make it stick. See §8.4.

questions.stem: Explain why so many changes 'did not stick'.
options: The refreeze step was skipped — new habits were not written into training, KPIs and rewards
The change was too small to be noticed by anyone, so people saw no reason to alter their habits at all
The employees were too young to understand why the organisation needed to change
The manager communicated too much, so the team stopped listening before the launch
questions.why: Refreezing is control; a change that is not measured, trained and rewarded was only announced. See §8.4.

questions.stem: Describe innovation as the chapter defines it.
options: Turning ideas into useful products, services or processes
Having many creative ideas and sharing them with the team in brainstorming sessions
Buying the newest technology before competitors do, so that the company looks modern
Copying what competitors do as soon as it works, so that the company is never left behind
questions.why: The key word is useful; creativity generates the idea, innovation applies it. See §8.5.

questions.stem: Differentiate creativity from innovation.
options: Creativity generates the idea; innovation implements it — and implementation is the harder half
Creativity is for artists and designers only; innovation is for engineers, product managers and the people who sell
They mean the same thing, and the chapter uses whichever word fits the sentence
Innovation generates the idea; creativity is the work of selling it to customers
questions.why: Everyone had the million-dirham idea; almost nobody did the four functions that turn it into a product. See §8.5.

questions.stem: Identify the four barriers that kill innovation inside organisations.
options: Fear of failure, resistance to change, lack of resources, rigid culture
Too many ideas, too much money, too many people and too much time on their hands
Customers, suppliers, competitors and government
Planning, organising, leading and controlling
questions.why: Organisations rarely lack ideas; they lack the conditions in which an idea survives its first week. See §8.6.

questions.stem: Explain the chapter's 'honest frame' about jobs and technology.
options: Jobs will mostly be reassembled, not abolished — routine goes to software, judgement and people stay with humans
All jobs will disappear within a generation, so students should prepare now for a world in which there is no paid work
Nothing will change in most jobs, because software has been promised for decades and never arrived
Only managers' jobs will disappear, because software can plan, organise and control better than people
questions.why: The accountant does less data entry and more advice; the manager does less reporting and more of the 70%. See §8.7.

questions.stem: Identify the skill the chapter calls the meta-skill for future managers.
options: Adaptability — it keeps the other skills current
Typing speed and software skills
Accounting, financial analysis and spreadsheet modelling
Memorising rules and procedures
questions.why: Adaptability is this whole chapter, made personal. See §8.8.

questions.stem: Analyse Kodak, which invented the digital camera in 1975 and went bankrupt in 2012, killed by digital cameras. Determine the explanation.
options: The success trap — it protected film against its own invention
It never saw digital coming, because its engineers were focused on improving film
It lacked engineers who understood digital technology well enough to build cameras
It had no customers for digital cameras, because the market did not exist until 2000
questions.why: Kodak literally built the future and still failed because today's successful business was too valuable to disrupt. See §8.1.

questions.stem: Classify a bookstore adding online sales.
options: A strategy change
A structure change
A people change
A process change
questions.why: A new direction is a change of strategy. See §8.1.

questions.stem: Identify the reason for resistance when an expert on the old system says 'with the new one I will look like a beginner'.
options: Fear of losing competence
Uncertainty about the future
Loss of control over the work
Laziness about learning
questions.why: 'Will I look incompetent with the new system?' — the fear of losing competence built over years. See §8.2.

questions.stem: Determine what a manager should do before announcing a change, according to the empathy flip.
options: Write the four sentences the team will say in the car park — fear, uncertainty, comfort, loss — and answer all four in the announcement
Announce quickly before rumours start, because the first version of the story is the one people remember
Send the manual first so that the team has read the details before the manager explains the reasons
Wait for the team to ask about the change, so that the manager answers the questions people actually have
questions.why: If you cannot answer all four, you are not ready to announce. See §8.2.

questions.stem: Analyse the company that installed a new system on Monday by email with a 40-page manual; by Friday staff were using the old spreadsheets. Determine the diagnosis.
options: No why (communication), no one consulted (participation), no practice (training), and the dip called 'resistance' (support)
The staff were lazy and used the new system as an excuse to avoid learning something new
The manual was too short to explain the system properly, so the staff could not use it
The system was too good for the company, so the staff could not keep up with it
questions.why: The fix is not a stricter email — it is the four tools, in order, before the next launch. See §8.3.

questions.stem: Select the tool that answers the fear of looking incompetent.
options: Training before launch, with safe practice time
A stricter email that makes clear the old system is no longer available
A bonus for every employee who uses the new system in the first month
A new manager who is more comfortable with the technology than the old one
questions.why: Fear of looking incompetent dies with competence. See §8.3.

questions.stem: Select the correct unfreeze action for a bookstore owner who refuses to change.
options: Show why the old way cannot continue — the falling numbers, the online competitor, the customer data
Install the new system quietly and hope that the owner learns to appreciate it once it is in daily use in the shop
Write the new process into the staff handbook so that the owner has to follow it
Celebrate the first success with the new system so that the owner sees it working
questions.why: People do not leave a comfortable room until they feel the cold. See §8.4.

questions.stem: Select the refreeze action for a change.
options: Write the new way into training, KPIs and rewards, and celebrate successes
Announce the change again in a longer email so that everyone has the details
Send the manual again with a reminder that the old way is no longer allowed
Return to the old spreadsheets until the team is ready for the new system
questions.why: Make it stick; skip this and the old way returns in a month. See §8.4.

questions.stem: Analyse a change where 'the unfreeze was an announcement, the change was a manual, and nobody refroze anything'. Determine the likely result.
options: The old way returns within a month
The change succeeds anyway, because the system is better and people will see that in time
The staff are promoted for adopting the new system so quickly after the announcement
Customers notice immediately that the service has improved and the ratings rise
questions.why: Most students find exactly this pattern in changes they have lived through. See §8.4.

questions.stem: Classify Careem, which owned no cars, and Airbnb, which owns no hotels.
options: Business-model innovation
New technology innovation
Improved service innovation
Not innovation
questions.why: The innovation was the model, not the technology inside it. See §8.5.

questions.stem: Classify a QR menu that replaced the laminated one during COVID and never left.
options: New technology innovation
Business-model innovation
A change of strategy
Resistance to change
questions.why: Small useful technology counts as innovation. See §8.5.

questions.stem: Analyse an organisation where one failed experiment ends careers and nobody experiments. Determine the manager's job.
options: Separate the failed experiment from the failed person; celebrate the well-run test that did not work
Punish failures harder so that people take more care before they experiment with the company's time and money
Stop all experiments until the organisation has a culture that can handle failure
Hire more creative people from outside, since the current staff are afraid to try
questions.why: Fear of failure is the first barrier; the manager's job is the conditions, not the ideas. See §8.6.

questions.stem: Select the manager's response to 'innovation' that is a poster, not a budget line.
options: A small protected budget and a few hours a week that nobody can reclaim
A bigger poster in the reception area so that staff and visitors see the commitment
A speech about creativity from the CEO at the start of the year
A new logo that shows the company is modern and open to new ideas
questions.why: Lack of resources is a barrier; protect time and money. See §8.6.

questions.stem: Analyse the registration redesign sample: pain points were mapped first, then the system proposed three clash-free schedules. Determine the lesson.
options: Circle the pain first; the idea comes second
Start with the most exciting technology and find a problem it can solve
Copy another university that has already redesigned its registration
Ask only the senior staff, because they know the system best
questions.why: Innovation starts from a real problem, not a gadget. See §8.6.

questions.stem: Compare two jobs: basic data entry and managing a team. Determine which is more likely to shrink and why.
options: Data entry — routine, predictable tasks are absorbed by software; managing people grows
Managing a team — software will replace managers because it can plan, organise and control
Both will disappear equally, because software can do routine work and lead people
Neither will change, because software has been promised for decades and never arrived
questions.why: Routine goes to software; judgement, care and creation grow. See §8.7.

questions.stem: Describe the Nokia example of the success trap.
options: Nokia perfected yesterday's phone while the market moved to smartphones
Nokia had no engineers who could build a smartphone
Nokia changed too fast and confused its customers with too many new models
Nokia was too small to compete with the companies that entered the market
questions.why: The better today's business performs, the harder it is to change. See §8.1.

questions.stem: Describe the 'uncertainty' reason for resisting change.
options: People do not know what the change means for them, so they hold on to what they know
People are lazy by nature and prefer not to learn anything new if they can possibly avoid it
People want more pay before they will accept any change in their work
People dislike the manager and resist to show that they do not trust her
questions.why: Uncertainty is one of the four honest reasons. See §8.2.

questions.stem: Describe the 'loss of control or status' reason for resisting change.
options: An expert in the old way fears becoming a beginner in the new one
People want a bigger office and resist until they are given one
People dislike computers and refuse to work with new technology
People are disloyal by nature and resist any change the company proposes to them
questions.why: Loss of status is one of the four reasons. See §8.2.

questions.stem: Explain the 'participation' tool.
options: Involve people in designing the change so they own it
Send a longer email about the change
Pay people a bonus to accept the change within the first month
Let people vote on whether the organisation should change at all
questions.why: People train for a design they had a say in. See §8.3.

questions.stem: Describe the unfreeze step.
options: Create readiness by showing why the old way cannot continue
Install the new system and switch off the old one
Write the new way into the KPIs so that it is measured from the start
Celebrate the first success so that the team sees the new way working
questions.why: People do not leave a comfortable room until they feel the cold. See §8.4.

questions.stem: Describe the refreeze step.
options: Make the change stick through training, KPIs, rewards and celebrated successes
Announce the change to the whole organisation at the same time
Show why the old way cannot continue, using the numbers
Buy the new system and install it before the staff are told anything about the change
questions.why: Refreezing is control applied to change. See §8.4.

questions.stem: Describe business-model innovation.
options: Changing how value is created and captured, such as Careem owning no cars
Inventing a new machine that does the work faster than the old one
Changing the logo and the brand so that the company looks different to customers
Hiring more staff so that the company can serve more customers at once
questions.why: The innovation was the model, not the technology. See §8.5.

questions.stem: Explain why implementation is the harder half of innovation.
options: Turning an idea into a product needs the four functions, which almost nobody does
Ideas are rare and precious, so the hard part is finding one that is worth implementing at all
Implementation is cheap, so companies rush it and get it wrong
Only engineers can implement, and most companies do not have enough of them
questions.why: Everyone had the idea; almost nobody did the work. See §8.5.

questions.stem: Describe the 'rigid culture' barrier.
options: 'We have always done it this way' stops ideas before they are tried
Too many budgets, so that nobody knows who pays for a new idea
Too much freedom, so that ideas are started and never finished
Too many customers, so that the staff have no time to think about new ideas
questions.why: Rigid culture is one of the four barriers. See §8.6.

questions.stem: Explain the phrase 'organisations rarely lack ideas'.
options: They lack the conditions in which an idea survives its first week
They have too few creative people, so the few ideas they have are protected
They have too many ideas to choose from, so none of them is given the resources it needs
Ideas are expensive to generate, so organisations should buy them from consultants
questions.why: The manager's job is the conditions, not the ideas. See §8.6.

questions.stem: Describe how a manager separates a failed experiment from a failed person.
options: Celebrate a well-run test that did not work, and learn from it
Punish the person who ran the test so that the next test is run more carefully
Hide failed experiments so that nobody loses confidence in the innovation programme
Stop experiments once one has failed, so that the organisation does not waste more money
questions.why: Fear of failure is the first barrier. See §8.6.

questions.stem: Describe the kind of work most likely to move to software.
options: Routine, predictable, repeatable tasks
Judgement in new situations
Caring for people who are worried or upset
Creating new things that have not existed before
questions.why: Routine goes to software. See §8.7.

questions.stem: Describe what happens to the accountant's job in the chapter's example.
options: Less data entry, more advice
The job disappears, because software can do accounting completely
Exactly the same job, because accounting rules do not change
Only data entry remains, because software gives the advice
questions.why: Jobs are reassembled, not abolished. See §8.7.

questions.stem: Explain why the manager's job grows rather than shrinks.
options: Judgement, motivation and people stay human while reporting goes to software
Managers cannot use software, so their jobs are protected from automation
Companies hire more managers when they install software, to supervise it
Software is too expensive for most companies, so managers will keep doing the reporting
questions.why: Less reporting, more of the 70%. See §8.7.

questions.stem: Explain why adaptability keeps other skills current.
options: It makes you keep learning as tools and jobs change
It replaces technical skill, so an adaptable person does not need to learn the tools
It is only for young people, who find it easier to learn new things
It is a personality type that some people have and others do not
questions.why: Adaptability is the meta-skill. See §8.8.

questions.stem: Describe the chapter's advice to a student about future skills.
options: Build judgement, people skills and the habit of learning — the parts software cannot do
Learn one tool very well and stop, because employers want specialists
Avoid technology, because the jobs that survive will be the ones software cannot touch for a long time
Wait to see what happens, because nobody knows which skills will be needed
questions.why: Adaptability made personal. See §8.8.

questions.stem: Identify the skill the chapter says will matter most in a fast-changing workplace.
options: Adaptability
Memorising procedures
Typing speed
Handwriting
questions.why: Adaptability keeps the rest current. See §8.8.

questions.stem: Classify a university moving from paper forms to an online registration system.
options: A technology and process change
A people change only, because the staff have to learn a new system
A strategy change, because the university is competing for students online
Not a change, because the forms contain the same information as before
questions.why: Technology and processes are two of the five things that can change. See §8.1.

questions.stem: Analyse a company with record profits that refuses to invest in its online shop. Determine the risk.
options: The success trap — today's success makes it hard to change
No risk — record profits prove that the company's current strategy is right
The online shop is illegal in some markets, so the company is right to wait
Customers prefer paper catalogues and shops, so the online shop would lose money
questions.why: Kodak and Nokia show where this leads. See §8.1.

questions.stem: Determine the resistance reason when staff say 'nobody told us what happens to our jobs'.
options: Uncertainty
Comfort with old ways
Loss of status
Laziness
questions.why: Not knowing what the change means is uncertainty. See §8.2.

questions.stem: Select the manager's best response to resistance.
options: Read it as information about what people are protecting and fix the plan
Treat it as disloyalty and make an example of the people who resist most
Ignore it and push the change through, because resistance always fades in time
Cancel the change, because a team that resists knows something the manager does not
questions.why: Resistance is information. See §8.2.

questions.stem: Select the tool that should come first when introducing a new system.
options: Communication — explain why
Training — show how
Support — be patient
Participation — ask for design ideas
questions.why: Nobody wants training for a change they do not understand. See §8.3.

questions.stem: Analyse a manager who punishes the performance dip in week two of a change. Determine the mistake.
options: Punishing the dip kills the change — support was needed
The dip means the change failed and the manager should return to the old way
Week two is too early to measure anything, so the manager should wait a month
Punishment speeds adoption, because people work harder when they fear the consequences
questions.why: Every real change has a dip. See §8.3.

questions.stem: Classify showing staff the falling numbers and the online competitor.
options: Unfreeze
Change
Refreeze
Innovation
questions.why: Create readiness by showing the cold. See §8.4.

questions.stem: Classify a hospital that redesigned its discharge process so patients leave two hours faster.
options: Improved process innovation
Business-model innovation
Not innovation — no new technology
A strategy change only
questions.why: Innovation is turning ideas into useful products, services or processes. See §8.5.

questions.stem: Analyse a student with a brilliant app idea who never builds it. Determine the chapter's view.
options: Creativity without innovation — the idea was never implemented
A complete innovation, because the idea was original
A business-model innovation, because the app would have changed how value is created
A technology innovation, because the idea was for a piece of software
questions.why: Innovation implements; creativity only generates. See §8.5.

questions.stem: Select the condition that lets ideas survive their first week.
options: Permission to run small tests without career risk
A bigger poster about innovation in reception
A stricter culture in which only approved ideas are discussed
Fewer meetings so that staff have more time to think about new ideas
questions.why: Separate the failed experiment from the failed person. See §8.6.

questions.stem: Classify answering routine customer emails.
options: Likely to be absorbed by software
Likely to grow for humans, because customers want a personal reply
Impossible to automate, because every email is different
Already extinct, because customers no longer send emails
questions.why: Routine goes to software. See §8.7.

questions.stem: Classify comforting a worried customer after a mistake.
options: Likely to stay human — care and judgement
Likely to move to software, because chatbots can say the right words
Already automated in most companies, with scripts for every situation
Not a job, because comforting customers is not part of any job description
questions.why: Judgement, care and creation grow. See §8.7.

questions.stem: Select the better career advice for a management student.
options: Build judgement and people skills, and learn new tools quickly
Avoid all software, because the jobs that survive will be the ones software cannot touch
Specialise only in data entry, because every company needs it
Wait until AI settles before choosing which skills to build
questions.why: Routine goes to software; judgement stays with humans. See §8.7.
